name: Kingdom of Galicia
info: A kingdom of the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula, formed in the partition of 910 and later joined to León and Castile, centred on the pilgrim city of Santiago de Compostela and dissolved in 1833.

facts.capital: Santiago de Compostela from the 11th century (Ordoño II was recognised king at an assembly of magnates in Lugo in 910)
facts.founder: Ordoño II, son of Alfonso III, who received Galicia in the partition of 910
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Asturias, divided among the sons of Alfonso III; earlier the Suebic kingdom (409–585) and the Visigothic province of Galicia
facts.successor: The provinces of Spain made by the liberal provincial division of 1833

t: Galicia was a distinct kingdom only in short interludes, under Ordoño II from 910, García II from 1065 and Alfonso VII, crowned at Compostela in 1111; otherwise it shared its kings with León and, from 1230, with Castile.
The tomb of Saint James the Great at Santiago de Compostela made the city the religious centre of the kingdom and the goal of the Way of St. James, a major international pilgrimage route.
From 1467 to 1469 the Irmandade, a brotherhood led by city dwellers with armies of armed peasants, governed the kingdom and demolished tens of the nobles' strongholds.
dyk: From 1423 the city of Zamora, in León but historically linked to Galicia, represented the Kingdom of Galicia in the Cortes, its deputies sitting at the monarch's right, until 1640, usually against the will and advice of the Galician cities.
ev: Alfonso III's lands are partitioned and Ordoño II is recognised king of Galicia at an assembly of magnates in Lugo
García II defeats and kills the rebel Count of Portugal, Nuno Mendes, at the Battle of Pedroso and takes the title King of Galicia and Portugal
The Galician high nobility crowns Alfonso VII king of Galicia at Santiago de Compostela, anointed by bishop Diego Gelmírez
Afonso Henriques defeats the troops of Theresa and Fernando Pérez de Traba at the Battle of São Mamede, the foundation of the future kingdom of Portugal
Ferdinand III succeeds Alfonso IX in León and Galicia, bringing Galicia permanently under the Crown of Castile
The Irmandiños rise and the Irmandade governs the kingdom until the exiled nobles return and defeat its armies
The Junta of the Kingdom declares itself the sovereign and supreme authority of Galicia during the Peninsular War
The Kingdom of Galicia and its Junta are dissolved in the liberal provincial division under the regent Maria Christina

sections.foundation:
The kingdom's roots lay in the 5th century, when the Suebi settled in the Roman province of Gallaecia, made Bracara Augusta (Braga) their capital and founded a kingdom known first as the Kingdom of the Suebi and later as the Kingdom of Galicia. It lasted from 409 until 585, when the Visigothic king Leovigild annexed it, and Galicia remained a distinct province of the Visigothic realm until the Battle of Guadalete in 711. From the mid-8th century the north-west was free of Arab presence and was gradually joined to the Christian state usually called the Kingdom of Asturias, whose Galician noblemen conquered and resettled southern Galicia and northern Portugal down to Coimbra in the 9th century.

When Alfonso III was forced by his sons to abdicate in 910, his lands were partitioned. García I received León, Fruela II the Asturian heartland, and Ordoño II the western lands, Galicia with the newly acquired lands of Coimbra, where he had already served as governor; he was recognised as king at an assembly of magnates in Lugo. From Galicia Ordoño raided the Islamic south and returned with riches and Muslim serfs. On García's death in 914 he also acquired León, and the kingdom of Galicia, though tied to León by its dynasty, remained a distinct political entity.
sections.socioeconomy:
In the Early and High Middle Ages the rural north became the leading part of Galicia. The local economy was subsistence, based on grain, beans and above all cattle; fruits, salt, wine, honey, olive oil, horses and iron came from particular districts, and long-range trade, generally in the hands of Hebrew merchants, was rare. Money was scarce, mostly old Suebi and Visigothic coins known as solidos gallicianos. War and pillage against Al-Andalus brought riches and Muslim serfs, and the pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela brought wealth and continental innovations, from shipbuilding to Romanesque art. The basic unit was the villa, centred on a church, which later became the rural parishes.

Ferdinand II and Alfonso IX granted charters to towns such as Pontevedra, Noia, Betanzos, A Coruña and Baiona, which attracted peasants, artisans and merchants and broke the autarky of earlier centuries; salted and dried fish, fish oil and wine went out through the seaports to England and the Mediterranean. City councils and artisan guilds arose, and Master Matthew's Portico da Gloria at Compostela showed the prosperity of the age. In 1348 the Black Death, known locally as A Mortaldade, reached the Galician ports and caused a severe and lasting economic crisis.
sections.military:
Galicia's nobles made and unmade kings. They crowned Ordoño IV at Santiago de Compostela in 958, resented the lack of Leonese help when the Normans raided Galicia from 968 to 970, and in 982 crowned Bermudo, who defeated Ramiro III at the battle of Portela de Areas. Almanzor, who led a brief resurgence of the Cordoban Caliphate, later raided Santiago de Compostela itself. The bishops of Iria and Compostela were warlords in their own right, holding the fortresses of a Norman march. In 1071 García II defeated the rebel Count of Portugal at the Battle of Pedroso, only to be driven into exile by his brothers; in 1111 the Galician knights supporting the boy Alfonso VII were defeated by the Aragonese infantry of Alfonso the Battler at Viadangos.

After the union with Castile, Galicia backed claimants against the crown: John of León in 1296, Ferdinand I of Portugal in 1369 and John of Gaunt, who landed at Coruña in 1386 and soon held the whole kingdom before plague decimated his army. The 15th century brought wars among noble houses holding castles across the country, and in 1467 the armies of the Irmandade, mostly armed peasants, demolished tens of strongholds before the nobles returned in 1469 with gunmen and mercenaries. The Catholic Monarchs then subdued the rebellious nobility with the Santa Hermandad, a Castilian police and military corps.
sections.governance:
Galicia was divided into bishoprics, and each bishopric into territories or counties whose rights of tax collection and government the king granted to a count, a bishop or a large monastery. In the Terra de Santiago, the fief of the bishops of Iria-Compostela, a bishop's vicar ran each territory and justice was given by a council of churchmen, knights and peasants. Galicia and León kept the Visigothic legal code, the Liber Iudicum, and their own Cortes, and public charters in the kingdom were written in Galician.

Under Castile the crown placed a meyrino maor in Galicia from 1231, replaced in 1251 by an adelantado mayor with greater powers. The kingdom lost its vote in the Cortes in the late 14th or early 15th century, and from 1423 Zamora spoke for it until 1640. The Catholic Monarchs sent a Governor of the Kingdom, an office first established in 1475, and in 1500 created the Real Audiencia del Reino de Galicia, a permanent royal tribunal. The Junta, or General Assembly of the Kingdom, from 1599 seven deputies of the provincial capitals, could grant or deny armies, ships and taxes and petition the king; in 1623 Galicia regained its vote in the Council of Castile.
sections.impact:
The shrine of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela gave Galicia a reach far beyond its size. The Way of St. James drew pilgrims from all over Europe, and Diego Gelmírez won the elevation of Compostela into an archdiocese in 1120, with jurisdiction over the old see of Mérida; the rivalry with Braga that followed made Braga the centre of the movement for Portugal's independence. In Al-Andalus Muslim sources, and among European Christians, the whole kingdom of León was known as Gallaecia or Galicia up to the 14th century.

Galicia gave the peninsula a language of culture. Galician-Portuguese, which contemporaries held to be one language, flourished in the 13th and 14th centuries, and some 2,000 cantigas survive in its love songs, songs of a woman for her beloved, songs of scorn and religious songs; Alfonso X the Wise was among its patrons. Galician was by far the most-used language of charters in the 13th to 15th centuries. The Codex Calixtinus and the Historia Compostellana came from the kingdom's thriving 12th century, and its chalice, first given to the King of Galicia in the English armorial Segar's Roll of 1282, became the modern coat of arms of Galicia.
sections.decline:
Ferdinand III's accession in 1230 began a gradual decline of Galicia's weight in the state. The court left Compostela, the kingdom lay on the periphery of a realm ruled from Toledo or Seville, and Alfonso X began a process that led, in the 15th and later centuries, to the replacement of Galician bishops, abbots and noblemen by Castilians. The withdrawal of John of Gaunt's armies in 1388 ended the nobles' and towns' attempts to secede from the Crown of Castile, and in the 15th century, with no king visiting before the Catholic Monarchs in 1486, the kingdom broke into rival fiefdoms. The Santa Hermandad and the Real Audiencia of 1500 brought it de facto under Castile; from about 1500 Castilian officials replaced the Galician elites and the Galician language was progressively discriminated against.

The wars of Philip II and his successors weighed on Galicia: the Inquisition from 1562, the English raids of Francis Drake in 1589, and, by the count of the kingdom's chronicler, more than 68,000 men served the crown between 1624 and 1659. Under the Bourbons the kingdom was governed by a Captain General within the Crown of Spain. Its Junta declared itself sovereign on 18 June 1808 and governed until the French conquest of 1809. The kingdom and its Junta lasted until the State Liberal Reform of 1833 and its provincial division; an uprising in 1846 restored Galicia's territorial unity for twenty-four days, but never the status of a kingdom.

summary: The Kingdom of Galicia, formed in 910 in the north-west of Iberia, was a separate realm only in brief interludes and otherwise shared its kings with León and Castile. Its pilgrim shrine at Santiago de Compostela, its nobles' revolts and its Galician-Portuguese poetry made it a force in medieval Iberia until Castilian centralization reduced it to a province, dissolved in 1833.
references: Richard A. Fletcher, Saint James's catapult: the life and times of Diego Gelmírez of Santiago de Compostela (1984)
Bernard F. Reilly, The kingdom of León-Castilla under Queen Urraca, 1109–1126 (Princeton U.P., 1982)
Bernard F. Reilly, The Kingdom of León-Castilla under King Alfonso VII, 1126–1157 (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1988)
Anselmo López Carreira, O Reino medieval de Galicia (A Nosa Terra, 2005)
José García Oro, Galicia en los siglos XIV y XV (Fundación Pedro Barrié de la Maza, 1987)
Manuel María de Artaza, Rey, Reino y representación. La Junta General del Reino de Galicia (CSIC, 1998)

pointDescs.910: In the partition of Alfonso III's lands Ordoño II receives Galicia and is recognised as king at an assembly of magnates in Lugo.
pointDescs.914: On the death of his brother García, Ordoño II also acquires León.
pointDescs.958: Galician nobles, allied with Fernán González of Castile, enthrone Ordoño IV at Santiago de Compostela; Sancho I reclaims the crown in 960.
pointDescs.982: The Galician nobility crowns Bermudo at Santiago de Compostela; he defeats Ramiro III and makes himself ruler of the Leonese kingdom.
pointDescs.1037: Bermudo III, who had ruled from his refuge in Galicia, is killed in battle and Galicia passes with León to Ferdinand.
pointDescs.1065: Ferdinand's death gives Galicia to his youngest son García II as a kingdom of its own.
pointDescs.1071: García II defeats the Count of Portugal at Pedroso and styles himself King of Galicia and Portugal.
pointDescs.1073: Imprisoned by Alfonso VI after returning from exile, García II dies in captivity in 1091; the reunion with León proves permanent.
pointDescs.1111: Alfonso VII is crowned king of Galicia at Santiago de Compostela; civil war follows across the realm.
pointDescs.1128: Afonso Henriques wins the Battle of São Mamede and Portugal begins to separate from Galicia.
pointDescs.1188: Alfonso IX proclaims himself king at Santiago de Compostela; his reign grants charters to towns along the coast and conquers much of Extremadura.
pointDescs.1230: Ferdinand III inherits León and Galicia, and the kingdom is joined to the Crown of Castile.
pointDescs.1301: John, proclaimed king of León and Galicia in 1296, abandons his claim, confirming the unity of the Crown of Castile.
pointDescs.1369: After the murder of Peter I, the Galician loyalists and cities invite Ferdinand I of Portugal to be their king.
pointDescs.1388: John of Gaunt renounces his claim; the withdrawal of the English ends Galicia's attempts to secede from Castile.
pointDescs.1467: The Irmandiños rise and the Irmandade governs the kingdom until 1469.
pointDescs.1500: The Real Audiencia del Reino de Galicia is established, integrating the kingdom de facto under the Crown of Castile.
pointDescs.1623: Galicia regains its vote in the Council of Castile in exchange for 100,000 ducats for a navy.
pointDescs.1808: The Junta declares itself the sovereign authority of the kingdom during the Peninsular War.
pointDescs.1833: The kingdom and its Junta are dissolved in the liberal provincial division.

notes: The article's lead says the kingdom and its Junta were dissolved by the regent in 1834; its 19th-century section says the kingdom existed formally until the State Liberal Reform of 1833. The register's end, 1833, is used; the ev date is 1833.
The register starts at 910, so the Suebic kingdom (409-585) and the Visigothic province are background in the foundation section only; the article treats them as the kingdom's origin.
The 1073 point is the year García returned from exile and was imprisoned; its description mentions his death in 1091 from the article.
The Fletcher reference has no publisher in the article (only an ISBN); left without one. Reference titles copied as the article gives them.
Military: 'Norman march' renders the article's 'a military Norman mark'.
